impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the enablement requirement under 35 U.S.C. § 112 permits broad method claims for treating headache with anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies where the functional genus of antibodies is expansive, and whether the panel's enablement analysis for method claims conflicts with Supreme Court precedent in Amgen v. Sanofi.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing of a panel decision upholding Teva's broad method-of-treatment patent claims against Eli Lilly's enablement challenge. Judge Dyk dissented, arguing the panel's holding sustains overly broad claims that undermine medical innovation and conflicts with Supreme Court enablement standards. The decision preserves the panel's more permissive enablement framework for method claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with broad method-of-treatment claims, particularly in the biopharmaceutical space, benefit from the more lenient enablement standard for method claims, which preserves broader patent protection for therapeutic antibody inventions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Competitors and generic/biosimilar manufacturers face broader blocking patents that may be difficult to design around, potentially delaying market entry and increasing licensing costs. The dissent signals ongoing uncertainty about the sustainability of this standard.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding plaintiff's trade secret damages expert and reducing the jury's breach of contract damages award, and whether sufficient evidence supported Ford's liability for trade secret misappropriation of licensed software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to consider two previously rejected damages models. The court reversed the reduction of the breach of contract jury award, reinstating the original verdict. It affirmed Ford's liability for misappropriating Versata's automotive configuration software trade secrets after Ford developed competing software while licensing Versata's products.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software licensors benefit from the affirmation that a licensee developing competing software using knowledge gained during the license relationship can constitute trade secret misappropriation. The reinstatement of the breach of contract jury award supports contract damages recovery.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that license third-party software and later develop in-house alternatives face heightened trade secret misappropriation risk. The remand for reconsideration of broader damages models could expose licensees to significantly larger damages awards.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an exclusive patent license agreement conveyed 'all substantial rights' sufficient to allow the licensee to sue for infringement without joining the patent owner, and whether the licensee's shift to an enforcement-only business model triggered the agreement's termination clause.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed dismissal, holding that TexasLDPC's exclusive license from Texas A&M University conveyed all substantial rights in the patents, giving TexasLDPC standing to sue without joining A&M. The court also held that shifting to a patent enforcement business model did not constitute ceasing business operations under the agreement's termination provisions.
impacts.positiveImplications: Exclusive licensees and patent assertion entities benefit from clarification that an exclusive license can be tantamount to an assignment for standing purposes, and that pivoting to enforcement-focused operations does not automatically terminate license agreements.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose the ability to challenge standing based on non-joinder of the patent owner when the exclusive license conveys sufficiently broad rights. Universities and other licensors may find it more difficult to retain meaningful control over patent enforcement.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform signal constellations for digital communications are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court erred in its infringement and damages analyses.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the district court's summary judgment of patent eligibility for certain claims of two patents related to non-uniform constellation technology used in broadcast communications, while affirming eligibility for claims of two other patents. The court also affirmed the denial of JMOL of non-infringement and the damages analysis. The case was remanded for further § 101 proceedings on the vacated claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in the communications/standards technology space benefit from the affirmance of eligibility for certain implementation-focused claims and the court's willingness to sustain substantial damages verdicts in standards-essential patent cases.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology implementers like LG face continued exposure to infringement liability for standards-compliant products. The partial vacatur creates uncertainty about the eligibility of more abstract signal-processing claims, requiring further litigation.

impacts.caseName: VDPP, LLC v. Volkswagen Group of America, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court abused its discretion in denying leave to amend, awarding attorney fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 as an exceptional case, and sanctioning plaintiff's counsel under 28 U.S.C. § 1927 for filing a frivolous patent infringement suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the dismissal of a patent infringement case without leave to amend and the award of over $207,000 in attorney fees to Volkswagen, finding the case exceptional under § 285. The court upheld the finding that plaintiff's counsel filed suit with deficient infringement allegations and without adequate pre-suit investigation. The sanctions holding reinforces accountability for patent plaintiffs and their counsel.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in weak patent infringement suits are protected by the court's willingness to award substantial fees and impose sanctions, deterring frivolous patent litigation and reducing defense costs.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent plaintiffs and their counsel face significant financial risk when filing infringement claims without thorough pre-suit investigation, particularly where related patents have been rejected on eligibility grounds.

impacts.caseName: Epic Tech, LLC v. Pen-Tech Associates, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court must provide sufficient analysis when denying Rule 11 sanctions and attorney fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 in a patent case where the asserted patent's related applications were rejected on § 101 grounds post-Alice.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the denial of sanctions and fee-shifting, holding the district court's order lacked sufficient detail for meaningful appellate review. The case involved an electronic sweepstakes patent asserted after related applications had been rejected under § 101 and after a related patent was invalidated in another district court. The ruling requires district courts to adequately explain their reasoning when declining to find a case exceptional.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants who prevail on § 101 invalidity grounds benefit from heightened scrutiny of district court denials of fee-shifting, increasing the likelihood of recovering defense costs in objectively weak patent cases.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent plaintiffs asserting patents with related applications rejected on eligibility grounds face increased risk that courts will be required to more carefully evaluate whether the case is exceptional, potentially leading to more fee awards against them.

impacts.caseName: Satius Holding, LLC v. Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims reciting a 'communications apparatus for transmitting electric or electromagnetic signals over air' with a 'coupler' matching impedances are indefinite, and whether the claims satisfy the enablement requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 112(a).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's indefiniteness ruling but affirmed the final judgment of invalidity on alternative enablement grounds. The court held that while the claim terms provided reasonable certainty to skilled artisans, the patent failed to enable the full scope of the claimed invention. This demonstrates the court's willingness to affirm invalidity on grounds not relied upon by the trial court.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent challengers benefit from the court's willingness to affirm invalidity on alternative grounds, providing multiple paths to invalidate overly broad patents even when the trial court's rationale is reversed.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face the risk that claims surviving an indefiniteness challenge may still be invalidated on enablement grounds, particularly when claims are drafted broadly relative to the disclosed embodiments.

impacts.caseName: AML IP, LLC v. Bath & Body Works Direct, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may dismiss a patent infringement case on both improper venue under 28 U.S.C. § 1400(b) and patent ineligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101 in the same order, rather than only dismissing for improper venue and transferring or allowing refiling.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal on both venue and § 101 grounds, holding that a court may address the merits of patent eligibility even after finding venue improper. The ruling allows courts to reach § 101 ineligibility determinations alongside venue dismissals, potentially preventing re-filing of weak patent cases in different venues.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants benefit from the ability to obtain simultaneous venue and eligibility rulings, preventing patent plaintiffs from simply refiling in a new venue with the same ineligible patents. This reduces repeated litigation costs.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent plaintiffs who file in improper venues risk not only dismissal but also a merits ruling on patent eligibility that could have preclusive effect, effectively ending their enforcement campaign.

impacts.caseName: NCS Multistage Inc. v. Nine Energy Service, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court correctly construed the claim term 'internal diameter' in oil and gas tool patents, and whether the jury's findings on direct and induced infringement were supported by substantial evidence.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the judgment of infringement of a patent directed to oil well casing float tools, finding error in the district court's claim construction of 'internal diameter.' The case involves significant oil and gas industry technology used in horizontal well completion, and the remand will require reassessment of infringement and potentially validity based on corrected claim construction.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers in the oil and gas industry benefit from rigorous claim construction review that may narrow patent scope, reducing exposure to infringement liability for competing downhole tools.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in the energy sector face the risk that broad claim constructions adopted at trial may be reversed on appeal, requiring costly retrials and potentially narrowing the scope of patent protection for drilling technology.
